issues.issue: The preamble makes Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. the Auction Agent acting "not in its individual capacity but solely as agent of WELLS FARGO BANK, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION (the 'Tmstee')" — the same entity is named as both principal and agent, so the capacity in which it acts and is liable is indeterminate. The garbled defined term "Tmstee" compounds the problem because the operative sections (e.g., 3.1(a)) all refer to "the Trustee."

The recital defines the four series collectively as the "Series 2004 Bonds" and then says the same set is "sometimes referred to together herein as the 'Series 2004 Auction Bonds'," equating two terms that Section 1.3(f) treats as distinct references. Which instrument-wide term governs an obligation is therefore open to construction.

"BD is to perform certain duties set forth herein" identifies no duties and gives no boundary to "certain duties," leaving open whether BD's obligations are exhausted by the express sections or extend further. The recital can be argued either to limit BD to enumerated tasks or to acknowledge a broader undertaking.

The recital makes the Auction Rate subject to two unstated escape hatches ("except as provided therein" and "except as otherwise provided therein") located in the Indenture, while Section 2.1(a)-(b) incorporates only the Auction Procedures and Settlement Procedures into this Agreement. What rate applies when the Auction Procedures do not produce one therefore cannot be resolved from the four corners of this instrument.

The recital says the Company "requested and directed" the Auction Agent to execute this Agreement, which sits awkwardly with Section 3.1(a)'s statement that the Auction Agent acts "solely as agent of the Trustee" and owes no duties to any other Person. Whose direction the Auction Agent answers to is thus contestable.

The recital that "the Auction Procedures require the participation of one or more Broker-Dealers" can be read as an undertaking that BD will participate in each Auction, while the operative terms (Section 2.1(d), which makes participation for BD's own account merely permissive) impose no obligation to bid. The recital may be argued to control or supplement those operative provisions.

"Unless the context clearly requires otherwise" supplies no test for when the context so requires, so every reference to purchase, sale or holding carries two possible referents (record ownership or beneficial interest). The escape clause is itself the ambiguity.

Section 1.3(f) deems references to "Bonds or Auction Bonds" to be references to each series of both "Series 2004 Bonds" and "Series 2004 Auction Bonds," although the recital defines those two terms as the same set of bonds. Whether obligations run series-by-series or to the whole issue is left unsettled.

The warranty is conditioned only on "the due authorization, execution and delivery hereof by the Auction Agent," omitting the Company, which is the third signatory under the preamble. The enforceability BD warrants is thus premised on an incomplete set of counterparties.

The subsection turns on "Initial Periods" and "Auction Rates," terms not defined in this Agreement but carried in from the Indenture, and it defines an "Auction" only as a periodic implementation of the procedures. It says nothing about an implementation that produces no rate, leaving the operative term's coverage of a failed auction unclear.

Wholesale incorporation of "all of the provisions" of the Auction Procedures and Settlement Procedures cannot be squared with Section 5.4, which declares this Agreement and connected instruments the entire agreement and disclaims other "agreements or understandings," nor with Section 3.1(b)'s undertaking of express duties only. Which body of terms controls a conflict between the incorporated procedures and the Agreement's own text is unaddressed.

"BD agrees to handle customer orders in accordance with its respective duties under applicable securities laws and rules" imports an unspecified and shifting body of external duty into the contract without defining it. Whether this converts regulatory obligations into contractual ones — and which rules qualify as "applicable" — is open.

The permission for BD to bid in Auctions for its own account cannot easily be squared with Section 2.3(b), which states that BD acts "for the purpose of implementing the Auctions (and thereby achieving the lowest possible interest rate on the Series 2004 Auction Bonds)." Proprietary bidding that supports or moves the clearing rate serves BD's interest and may defeat the stated purpose of the very next section.

The 9:30 a.m. deadline carries no time zone and "other electronic communication acceptable to the parties" states no standard for acceptability or how acceptance is shown. Whether a given transmission satisfied the notice duty is therefore contestable.

The confidentiality undertaking is subject to a catch-all exception — disclosure whenever failure "would expose the Auction Agent to loss, liability, claim, damage or expense for which it has not received indemnity satisfactory to it" — that is broader than the specific court-order and unlawfulness exceptions preceding it and may swallow the covenant. The self-judging "satisfactory to it" supplies no measurable limit.

"As of the opening of business on such date" does not say whether "such date" is the Business Day preceding the Auction Date on which notice is given or the Auction Date itself. The content of the notice — the change being reported — turns on which date is meant.

The BMA sentence sets the Submission Deadline at 11:30 a.m. "instead of 1:00 p.m.," but the schedule table sets the deadline at 1:00 p.m. and at 11:00 a.m. for a daily Auction Period, so the deadline on a shortened trading day with a daily Auction Period is internally inconsistent. "Unless the Auction Agent is instructed otherwise" also does not say by whom.

The parenthetical purpose "and thereby achieving the lowest possible interest rate on the Series 2004 Auction Bonds" cannot be squared with Section 2.1(d), which permits BD to bid in Auctions for its own account. Whether the parenthetical is an enforceable obligation owed to the Company or mere explanation of BD's marketing role is exactly what the two provisions leave in doubt.

"Other relevant documents prepared for the purpose of disclosure to Potential Owners" has no boundary: it does not say who decides relevance or which offering or auction-practice disclosures are covered. The delivery duty also arises only "upon request," without saying whose request.

Orders must be "substantially in the form" of Exhibit B or in such other form "as may be reasonably acceptable to the Auction Agent," with no standard for substantial conformity or reasonable acceptability. Whether a non-conforming Order is valid is left to argument.

The Auction Agent's discretion not to accept a notice received after 3:00 p.m. collides with Section 2.6(a), which provides that any delivery departing from Auction results "shall be of no effect unless and until the Auction Agent shall have been notified ... in accordance with the terms of Section 2.3(d)." A refused late notice would leave a completed transfer permanently of no effect.

The written confirmation duty arises only "if so requested" and only "as soon as reasonably practicable," neither of which is defined or bounded. Whether the Auction Agent has breached its notice obligation cannot be measured against these terms.

This bare duty to notify BD of any schedule change duplicates, without the timing limit, the notice obligation already imposed by Section 2.3(a) (notice "prior to the close of business on the Business Day next preceding the first Auction Date on which any such change shall be effective"). Which timing requirement governs is unclear.

"Take such other action as is required of BD pursuant to the Settlement Procedures" is an open-ended obligation whose content lies wholly outside this Agreement in a document incorporated by Section 2.1(b). The scope of BD's settlement duties therefore cannot be determined from the provision.
